interactions.title: Shakun’s restored protection
lines: DM: It seems that overnight, the news of Agata's death and the restoration of safety to Karawa, even though many don't know exactly how that safety is provided, has traveled throughout the few people who remain in the village. And news has already left, riders have already left to Tokra to try to tell the refugees that it's safe to come home.

DM: And you awaken to a bounty of what little meager fruit and meat is still available in town piled outside your camp in thanks. Everybody who you see, as you begin the morning riding out of town, greets you with praise and joy and thanks for your deeds bringing—bringing protection back to this part of the world.

DM: Cintra and her daughter Jumi, now safe back in the Temple of Shakun, with Shakun's heart with them, don't emerge to greet you as you leave, but all of you can still feel her presence growing stronger and more forceful overnight, as the web of Shakun's power has grown and connected to the restored heart.

DM: With Seeker and Wellby having asked to have your connections to the heart cauterized and ended, so as not to be a continual drain on its power, can feel this sort of sense, this magic slowly fading in your consciousness as the memories of this web among the Mystai become hard for you to concentrate on. Other memories of your adventures remain, but when you try and recall the details of—

DM: What Shakun's heart is, you find your mind slipping away from that knowledge. Kenzo and Drikod, intending to be fully bound into this web of power when—when you return and can go through the full initiation ritual, can feel it growing stronger, becoming more real and real and substantial than you could have imagined before, and you can actually almost see the sort of, um, sort of energy creeping out across the land and inching out from Karawa towards the border, and with each pulse of the heart this power stretches a little bit further, and you can feel your connection to it begin to ebb a little bit.

before: DM: So, bringing us back into town.

DM: As the days are growing long in the desert of Dunmar, the heat reaching its hottest point, the dry desert terrain around you longing for the relief that the summer thunderstorms that come following the [garbled] monsoons bring.

DM: Dawn comes to a very changed Karawa. You awake in your camp on the edge of the oasis, still the center public square of Karawa, to the sounds of hope: the chatter of people mixing mud into bricks to dry in the sun, the bang of hammers as rubble is broken into smaller pieces to be cleared or reused for new construction, the regular click of shovels as dirt is dug for building materials.
after: DM: As dawn broke, you said goodbye to Candrosa, who brought a small cart—leading a donkey pulling a small cart laden with what supplies he could find and, just in case it turns out to matter, like food's kind of short in town.

DM: So whatever rations you had before were swept away as you never actually, like, you know, your camp was abandoned in the desert, but Baxter, despite his cleverness and dexterity, was not able to pack up everything you had left with the horses.
DM: So just put yourself at five rations for everybody. Or I'll say six rations which is just enough to get there and back if you don't dawdle.
Seeker: What where's that?
DM: I mean, it's just on your equipment, just give yourself six rations. I'm just to give you a little time pressure not to go haring off into the desert without a plan.

interactions.title: Candrosa’s farewell and directions
lines: DM: As dawn broke, you said goodbye to Candrosa, who brought a small cart—leading a donkey pulling a small cart laden with what supplies he could find and, just in case it turns out to matter, like food's kind of short in town.

DM: So whatever rations you had before were swept away as you never actually, like, you know, your camp was abandoned in the desert, but Baxter, despite his cleverness and dexterity, was not able to pack up everything you had left with the horses.

DM: Candrosa also brought what stories he could gather of Agata's lair, and few are willing to speak openly of this or admit they had gone, and especially among the Mystai, he believes that, in fact, few had, that few or none had actually been to the lair of those who were in town and you did not want to wait for refugees to return and the sort of larger population and try to circle back so that you could, you know, give—

DM: Ask for more information, but he did report a few things that were relevant. So one thing is everybody, the sort of common understanding that many people say, or the rumor that many have heard, is that the approach to Agata's lair is lined with a row of dead trees in the desert. And when she was alive supplicants asking for her favor would be led to these dead trees, to this path by, um, by flies or scorpions who would appear as a swarm out of the desert when you traveled south from Bas Udda and lead you to this path. But Candrosa suspects, and you suspect as well, that this was some—some sign of the will of Agata and is probably no longer there, but the line of trees may remain and would be a landmark. The other thing that Candrosa says is the lair can only be approached from the north. If you circle around and approach it from the south, it is not there, what that means, nobody really knows, but those who have gone exploring, trying to find a secret hidden path to Agata's lair, have never succeeded and found just dry desert instead.

DM: So now, as you ride out of Karawa with that information in the dawn light, there's no avoiding the thoughts of the journey ahead, that trial, potential trials of Agata's lair, and what may be hidden there, what may need to be recovered or protected before wanderers in the desert stumble upon it for good or ill. Who is trapped there, turned to wood and bound in a curse tied to the small carved statues you carry now, recovered from Agata's person? Can they be saved? And what dangers or traps prepared for unwary guests may still lurk in her lair now, days after her death?

interactions.title: The necklace’s tongues and the cost of using it
lines: Seeker: Seeker's been kind of poking at them disgustedly, but now one morning of the journey puts on the purple goggles and and gazes at them intently. He sort of sets the Tongue down in the dust and puts the goggles on to stare at them from a foot away.
Kenzo: And just, like, kind of crouching also, like not getting close, but just with the staff, like looking at it, like.

DM: So, as you—as you do this um, you—you get a sense. You get a sense from the necklace that each of these tongues was once in a creature and that they—those creatures were ritually slaughtered to produce this item.
DM: And what it does, is it is literally a necklace of tongues. Each—each dead humanoid or some of them are not actually humanoids. Each dead—let me see what languages are. Um.
DM: So each creature that was killed for to create this necklace gave the ability to speak their native tongue to whoever is wearing and attuned to the item.

DM: And as you stare at it with the goggles, you can see the tongue is kind of expanding a little and growing and becoming flesh again, and you can't recognize every one, but there are a number of human tongues, there's one that's clearly a halfling. There's one that seems to be some kind of giant bird. There's one that looks like one of those gnoll creatures you killed once. A few more that you can't readily identify, but you guess there's at least, there's one, two, three, four, five. There are 14 tongues in this necklace.
Kenzo: It's that plus the Scepter of Command.
Delwath: No, that, well, the Scepter of Command speaks its commands in all possible tongues.
Seeker: So they just have different.

DM: Useful. So what this does is while you're wearing and attuned to the necklace, you can speak and understand any language that is the native tongue of a creature whose tongue is part of the necklace.
Delwath: That's really useful but also.
DM: The tongues are added to the necklace by a ritual that requires eight hours of time and the sacrifice of a living creature.

Seeker: Whoa, heavy. Um, I—I pick it up and stare at it, thinking about if I were to wear it, what I would need to do to it first. Maybe I could wrap it up in leather or something like that to make it hide the tongues a little bit.
Seeker: Cover it up. Because I'm a little uncomfortable with it, but the the power of it is evident.
DM: There is that. It's on D&D Beyond, there's the item.
Wellby: Wellby will say, “I want to take the halfling tongue off of that.”
Wellby: Right to use a creature like that, besides, it's a closed language, we only teach it to the people who want to know.

Seeker: If I were to put this on right now I could reply in some snarky way to your comment in the Tongue but I think we might perhaps rethink the use of this, all together, then, because these are remains of thinking beings after all, attached to this necklace not just to have fun, but conscious minds that could speak languages of all sorts represented here. Perhaps we should simply give it a burial.
Delwath: I think the—what we should do: We should show it to the mirror and find out whose tongues they were and how they died.
Delwath: And remove those, like halfling, for whom it feels—That the demon creatures that we've been hunting for the last three months, I cannot find any sympathy for that, right?
Kenzo: Agree. Well, the ability to be able to communicate with them and learn more and what's happened also.
Delwath: To the extent that Abyssal, the fiends from other planes, I cannot find sympathy for them either, right, to the extent that Agata sacrificed our enemies to this, so.

Seeker: I say, Delwath, you're making a moralistic argument on the basis that certain categories of creatures, because of the actions of creatures in general in that category, deserve to have the remains desecrated of individual creatures who may not have participated in those acts. Perhaps that's too nuanced an argument.
Wellby: What? Evil is genetic in this world.
Delwath: Cha'mutte was trying to change that, but she was defeated.

DM: I mean, okay, so you would all know that, like there is definitely—there are definitely some things, like, I mean, demons are evil, those are not separable things. There are no demons that, like, you know, reject their demon heritage and try to do good, right?
DM: Because those are fundamentally tied together. They're not—they're not from this world; they're from another plane and the whole essence of that plane is evil.
Delwath: But presumably a fiend who tried to reject the essence of their plane would either disintegrate or become something else.

DM: Would cease to be a fiend, right, like. It's not to say that it's completely impossible, it's to say that they couldn't remain a fiend and do that. They could seek redemption, but it would have to involve becoming something that wasn't a fiend, and—whereas, for example, you do know that while you've heard rumors for example of orcs that have thrown off their divine shackles and are farmers. Farmers.
DM: Right so whether evil is genetic depends on what kind of evil you're speaking of.
Kenzo: Well, I certainly like the idea of using the mirror to understand more about the nature of each of these tongues before we make any decisions.

Delwath: I also think some of these languages may help us in the short, I think the halfling, perhaps dwarvish tongues should be removed before we do anything. And perhaps the Chardonian and Dunmari, the human tongues as well.
Seeker: Is there a dwarven tongue?
DM: Yeah so the list of language.
Delwath: Of looking at this, and so what, that thing, I'm looking at the link Tim posted, which has the list of—
DM: That's all for the list of tongues here.
Seeker: Oh, my gosh that's crazy.
Seeker: Investigate—investigating the construction of the thing, is there a way to safely remove some tongues? Maybe you can reverse?

DM: Make an Investigation check, or Arcana, I think they're the same plus for you. Yes. You can definitely, so each tongue is strung on this piece of copper, like just a copper wire, and there's a clasp at the back, and you can see that the tongues are sort of shriveled onto the wire, but could certainly be just cut and removed, and as far as you can tell you don't think that would affect the magic of the tongues that remain. Now it's not trivial to, the humans, dwarves and halflings you can identify. Um, it's not straightforward to tell which tongue matches with which other language.
Delwath: Presumably, which human is which right?
DM: You can't tell which human's which at all, right? You can tell the three human tongues, there's a dwarven tongue, there's a halfling tongue, and there's a bunch of stuff you don't really know.
Delwath: Elves are hard to find and harder to kill.
Seeker: They don't voluntarily part with their—
DM: Parts. It's a good thing Agata didn't find Delwath. If Agata had found Delwath instead of Pava and Avaras.
Kenzo: Wandering in the desert oh yeah. Yeah yeah yeah.
Seeker: Pre-pre campaign, I will quickly modify the necklace removing—it's like how do I choose?
Kenzo: They were just going to, [garbled], removing all of the other tongues just to do it.
Wellby: Wellby's gonna be pretty insistent about the halfling.
Seeker: I will remove the halfling tongue. I will stay open about future modifications.
Delwath: I think you should remove the dwarven as well. You speak?
Drikod: The dwarven tongue could be from a different, the dwarf could have known another language, right? Is it the language of the keeper of the tongue? Or is it the racial languages?
DM: It's the—Seeker, your understanding from the magic of the item is, it is the native tongue of the creature. The native language of the creature whose tongue is attached to the necklace.
Seeker: So there must be multiple native dwarven languages, no?
DM: There's just one dwarven language.
Seeker: Then I can safely remove that one as well, yes.

Seeker: To store the tongue necklace, sans halfling tongue, in my pack. In the event of an emergency, we may need to use it, regardless of the moral concerns. In the event of a less emergent linguistic need, perhaps we can consider that time.
Wellby: If we could use it to save a life perhaps we could use an evil thing to prevent—
Seeker: In exchange for a contract. Okay, I agree, I stash the tongues, hoping to silence them temporarily at least.

Unknown: Of course.
Delwath: Delwath reach into thin air and pull it out of the sky and hand it to you. Don't know if this is the same one. Whatever weapon I'm thinking of just is there when I reach.

It's not—I don't even know if it's the same every time.
Kenzo: If you marked it and put it back in, can you pull out the same one?

Delwath: I haven't tried, although, I mean, Delwath's weapons aren't regular weapons, right? They're like pure blackness that look completely unreal and hard to mark. Delwath will take a sword. Any ideas how to mark this, Kenzo?
Kenzo: Can you put other objects that aren't these shadow weapons in there, into that other plane?
Delwath: Yeah, put a, tie a string around.
DM: And then, and then make—
DM: Take it, the string just falls to the ground.
Delwath: Out when I put it back the string just falls to the ground yep.
Seeker: And the weapons are substantial; they're made of some physical material.

Delwath: They—they have the weight, such that they don't throw you off, but I don't know if they're really made of a physical material, I mean, is—is magical force a physical material? [garbled] that they act with the force of magic, not with the force of a sword.
Delwath: The sword doesn't cut you because it's sharp, it cuts you because it's magic.
Delwath: I've never thought to try. Science science night.
Delwath: Actually that's it right yeah. I'll conjure a dagger and drop it in a waterskin. Does it float?

DM: Mean you don't—I guess you've got—you must have like a barrel of water in your—on your horse. No, it's like a normal dagger, it sinks to the bottom. Seems to have the weight of, of a normal dagger.
Delwath: Ariel jada was my character in high school, if you're mashing the button.
Seeker: And this veil into this shadow world that you can simply reach your hand through is always—is always traveling around with you, you have access to it at any moment?

Delwath: Seems like it's always there, yes. The Shadow Realm, I think, is always next to us, it's always present, like a mirror of Taelgar, at least that's my theory. Always, always here, wherever I get—wherever anybody is, and I just can reach through it.
Seeker: I'm glad to learn of these things, but I must admit, it does not fit in my system of the world as it stands, I will need to revise once again.
Drikod: Because I can't imagine a place without nature. This, this—it's very disconcerting for him as he's listening in the background to this. But.

Delwath: To be honest, I know very little about how this—this works, I feel the energy of my magic come from the same source mediated, perhaps through creature, uh, this being that has spoken to me once or twice.
Drikod: Does it have to do weapons? Can you pull other things?

Delwath: Yeah. It's not—it's an armory. It's not a, it's not a, it's not just a place of all things. But of course my little, create a floating hand, I mean, you see—creates hands the same, I feel the same energy flowing through me when I do that as I do, when I pull the—pull the weapon from this shadow realm. It's the same source of power somehow.

Seeker: It could be used quite easily, for instance to master the group itself should someone at any given moment, decided that that was necessary.
Kenzo: Hey Tim. Yeah, what's the thing that, because Kenzo can read when Delwath's lying and telling the truth and see lies now?
Seeker: In the meantime, while he's reading that I'm using Ai to generate an image of the necklace of tongues and let me tell you—
Kenzo: Are we riding horses? Are we walking? What are we doing right now? We're talking and riding horses yeah.

Kenzo: Okay okay okay. Oh geez. This fucking scepter.
Drikod: Why are you—why not just destroy it? It's really more evil than one halfling tongue.

Delwath: Lot of, why is it [garbled]? I'm just trying to find the right—
Kenzo: Is like is like slowly as like gripping his staff, like a little more tightly.
